headline: Your IGF-1 is higher
punch: Three studies. Same dose, different pattern.

headline: One number, every protocol
body: So the chain everyone recites is simple and it sounds airtight. GH raises IGF-1, IGF-1 drives growth, therefore push IGF-1 as high as you can tolerate and track it on bloodwork to see how you are doing. Every protocol you will read is built on that chain. | There is a set of experiments from the eighties and nineties that breaks the last link, and they are old, clean, and almost never cited by anyone selling you a protocol.
punch: What if higher IGF-1 is not more growth?

headline: The setup
body: These studies all use *hypophysectomised* rats, meaning the pituitary has been surgically removed so the animal produces zero GH of its own. Every molecule of growth hormone in that animal is the one you put there, which removes the biggest confounder in the field. | Then you give the exact same total daily dose two different ways. As a steady continuous infusion. Or in pulses: **8 pulses a day, 5 minutes each, every 3 hours**. Identical hormone. Only the shape of delivery changes.
punch: _Dose held constant. Only the pattern moves._

headline: Clark 1985
body: At the low dose the result is about as stark as experimental biology gets. **Continuous infusion at 12 mU per day gave no net gain in body weight at all**, while the same dose given in a pulsatile manner produced significant body growth, P < 0.05. | Same amount of hormone, same animals, same period. One delivery pattern grew the animal and the other did literally nothing. Analysis of variance confirmed pulsatile was significantly more effective than continuous.

headline: Isgaard 1988
body: This one went after bone directly rather than body weight. A pulsatile pattern was more effective than continuous at stimulating **longitudinal bone growth**, P < 0.01. | Then they looked at the tissue level. In skeletal muscle, pulsatile GH at 3-hour intervals induced a **3 to 5 fold increase in IGF-1 mRNA**, while continuous treatment **exerted no effect** whatsoever. Not a smaller effect. No effect.
punch: Pulses built tissue. The drip did not.

headline: The liver does not care
body: Here is the part that explains the mechanism. In that same study there was **no significant difference** between pulsatile and continuous GH on hepatic IGF-1 mRNA. The liver produced its IGF-1 either way, happily, regardless of pattern. | So the tissues that need the pulse are the growth plate and the muscle, the ones manufacturing their own *local IGF-1*. The endocrine organ is pattern-blind and the target tissues are not. That single contrast is why serum IGF-1 fails as a marker.
punch: ==The liver ignores the pattern. The growth plate does not.==

headline: Bick 1992
body: They measured serum IGF-1 and growth in the same animals, which is the comparison nobody else made. Serum IGF-1 came out **higher after continuous** GH treatment. | And despite that, the pulsatile group **induced a greater body weight gain than the same dose infused continuously**. Higher blood IGF-1 in one group, more actual growth in the other group, same experiment, same dose. The marker and the outcome pointed in opposite directions.
punch: _The number went up and the animal grew less._

headline: One line from the authors
body: They wrote it themselves, and it is the cleanest sentence in this whole series: **receptor, GH-BP, and IGF-I are stimulated more by continuous GH delivery, whereas growth is enhanced more by pulsatility**. | What this means is that serum IGF-1 is not a scoreboard for growth. Under a continuous delivery pattern it rises precisely while the growth falls. Anyone optimising that number without knowing its pattern is optimising something that can move the wrong way.
punch: ==Serum IGF-1 is a marker, not the mechanism.==

headline: Why would that happen?
body: Bick measured hepatic GH receptors directly and found them **higher after continuous delivery**, with occupied receptors highest right after a pulse and lower 90 minutes later. | A constant signal keeps receptors occupied and the tissue stops responding to it, which is ordinary receptor biology and happens with almost every hormone. The trough between pulses is not downtime or wasted hormone. The trough is the thing that makes the next peak work at all.
punch: The gap between pulses is doing work.

headline: The human trial
body: Now the honest part, because this is where the rat data stops. Lundberg 2015 randomised children to the same daily GH dose given **once daily or split into two injections**, 67 µg/kg once versus 33 µg/kg twice. | The result: **no differences in height gain** between them. The split did nothing measurable. That is a real human randomised result and it has to be dealt with rather than ignored.
punch: _One human test of splitting the dose. It changed nothing._

headline: A depot is not a pulse
subhead: WHY THAT IS NOT A CONTRADICTION
body: Look at what the rat pulse physically was. Intravenous, **5 minutes long, 8 times a day**, producing a sharp spike and a real trough between each one. Now look at a subcutaneous injection: a depot under the skin releasing slowly over hours. | Splitting one slow depot into two slow depots does not create a pulse. It creates two slightly smaller slow depots with no trough between them. What this means is that the human trial tested dose splitting, which is a different intervention from pulsatility.
punch: The experiment that matters in humans has not been run.

headline: What actually holds up
body: Three things survive. Delivery pattern changed growth independently of total dose, repeatedly, in multiple labs. The liver and the growth plate respond to pattern completely differently, which is the mechanism. And serum IGF-1 moved opposite to growth, so it is not a scoreboard. | What does not survive is anyone claiming they have the human protocol. One trial split a dose in two and found nothing, and that is the entire human evidence base on this question.
punch: ==Stop reading IGF-1 as your growth number.==
